sections.text: Methods are functions that belong to a type. You write them inside an impl block. The first parameter, self, is the value the method is called on.
&self borrows the value to read it. &mut self borrows it to change it. Plain self takes ownership.

Every function in an impl block is an associated function: it belongs to the type. The ones that take self are methods, called with a dot. The ones without self are called with :: and are often used as constructors named new:
You've already used associated functions: String::from is one.
Inside an impl you can write Self instead of the type name, e.g. fn new() -> Self. Method calls auto-reference, so r.area() works whether r is a value or a reference.

exercise.prompt: main already calls r.perimeter(), but Rectangle has no such method yet. Add a method perimeter(&self) -> u32 to Rectangle that returns 2 * (width + height). It should print: area 12, perimeter 14

tests.label: The program prints the area and the perimeter

hints: Look at how area is written inside impl. Your new method follows the same pattern, so copy its shape.
Add fn perimeter(&self) -> u32 inside the impl block. Use self.width and self.height in the calculation.
The body is 2 * (self.width + self.height), with no semicolon after it, so it is the value the method gives back.

quiz.question: Where do you write methods for a struct?
quiz.explanation: Methods go in an impl block for the type. The struct definition lists only fields, and main is just a function that uses the type.

quiz.question: Which self should a method that changes the value take?
quiz.explanation: A method that changes the value needs &mut self, which borrows it mutably. &self only lets you read, and a function with no self isn't a method on the value.

quiz.question: How do you call an associated function new on Account?
quiz.explanation: An associated function is called on the type with ::, so Account::new(). The dot is for methods on a value, and new Account() is a syntax from other languages. In Rust new is just a normal function name.
